citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility is failing to maintain a program of adequate veterinary care that includes the use of appropriate methods to
prevent and control diseases and injuries.
Helmeted Curassow (DWA2114/10AB114) and Many Banded Aracari (16HO11/Cage A3B #4), have moderately long
nails that are overdue for a trim. Overgrown nails may impact a bird's ability to perch appropriately, which can be
detrimental to their health and well-being.
Each dealer or exhibitor shall establish and maintain programs of adequate veterinary care that include the use of
appropriate methods to prevent, control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries.
Correct by August 31, 2026.

citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility failed to communicate the following problems of animal health to their attending veterinarian:
A Blue-Billed Curassow (2H5048) was injured by a bird in an adjacent enclosure. The bird sustained a one-inch laceration
to the top part of its beak. The Blue-Billed Curassow’s injury had not been communicated to the attending veterinarian.
Prompt assessment of an animal needs to be made to minimize pain and suffering. Providing an animal with veterinary
care and following the guidance of the attending veterinarian allows for the correct diagnosis to be made to better treat,
control, or prevent disease. Each dealer or exhibitor shall establish and maintain programs of adequate veterinary care
that include the use of appropriate methods to prevent, control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries.
Correct by August 31, 2025.

The facility stores bird food and supplements in a manner that does not protect them from contamination and vermin
infestation. A plastic container in the food prep area holding bird supplements contained two spray bottles of cleaning
supplies. Inspectors observed a bottle of hand sanitizer on a shelf above an open bag of bird supplement and a bottle of
bleach on the same shelf with fresh fruit that was prepped for the birds. The facility is storing numerous pallets of bird feed
in the Aquarium’s general storage area for human food receptacles (drinking cups), fertilizer, machinery, and other
equipment. Two bags of bird feed were stored directly on the floor. The current arrangement of the food among the non-
food equipment and supplies makes it difficult to clean underneath and around the food pallets.
Improper storage of food and food supplements may expose them to contamination, spoilage, and vermin infestation.
Correct by storing the supplies off the floor, away from the walls and in a manner that protects the supplies from
deterioration, spoilage, contamination, and vermin infestation.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

The primary enclosures for multiple species contain sharp points from the holes made in the wire fencing. In cage 1A in
the indoor area containing two adult Birds of Paradise, inspectors observed a 3” by 2” hole with sharp points from the wire
fencing. Cage 2 in the indoor area containing two adult Curl Crested Aracaris had a 2” by 2” hole with sharp points. Cage
3 in the indoor area containing two adult Ivory Billed Aracari had a 2” by 2” hole with sharp points. In cage 4 of the indoor
area containing two adult Cocks of the Rock, inspectors observed an approximately 2” screw sticking out of the perch in
front of the food and water receptacles. Cage 6 of the indoor area containing an adult Ivory Billed Aracari had a hook
hanging on the enclosure with the sharp point facing towards the birds. In cage 9 of the indoor area, a zip tie above the
enclosure door was cut in a manner resulting in a sharp edge. In an outdoor cage containing two adult turkeys, the
enclosure wire was cut resulting in 1” sharp points. In Aviary 20, there was an enclosure containing one adult Green
Aracari with two 2” by 2” holes. Aviary 17 cage 7 containing a Harpy Eagle had two wooden boards at the back left corner
of the enclosure showing signs of rot with exposed nails with sharp points. In Aviary 3A cage 14 containing one Raggiana
Bird of Paradise, inspectors identified a loose self-tapping screw on the floor of the enclosure and the black plastic planter
for the tree was breaking apart in several areas creating sharp points.
Primary enclosures must be kept in good repair. They must be constructed and maintained so that they have no sharp
points or edges that could injure the birds.
The specific sharp points listed above were corrected by the end of the inspection.

The primary enclosure housing for various species of birds contained uncovered electrical outlets with exposed wires,
exposed electrical wiring for the internal camera system and loose zip ties with a sharp edge. Outdoor cage 6 containing
two adult Ivory Billed aracaris had camera wires hanging into their enclosure. Indoor cage 9 had loose zip ties that posed
entanglement risk for the birds contained therein. Cage 1 containing two Many Banded Aracaris had a camera wire
hanging into their enclosure. Outdoor cage 9 containing two adult Blue-Billed Curassows had an uncovered electrical
outlet with exposed wires that was confirmed to be live. There was an exposed electrical wire in cage 7 with 2 adult
Helmeted Curassows. Aviary 2, cage 17 holding two adult Black Mandible Toucans had loose zip ties that posed
entanglement risk. Outside of Aviary 12, an enclosure with one adult Lettered Aracari had a loose zip tie that poses an
entanglement risk. Aviary 12 cage 15 had a long live electrical wires hanging into the enclosure containing two adult Curl
Crested aracaris. Cage 8 D and E in the roof top area, containing two adult Spectacled Owls had exposed live electrical
wiring present above their nest box. Cage 26 with two adult Andean Cock of the Rocks and one adult Scarlett Cock of the
Rock had a loose zip tie creating a large loop with approximately 2-inch diameter is an entanglement risk. In Aviary 20,
there was a cage containing two juvenile Wattled Curassows where approximately 18 inches of the wire netting covering
their enclosure box had disconnected from the edges which was easily lifted by USDA inspectors during the inspection
and could serve as escape or entrapment risk. Uncovered electrical outlets and the exposed wiring are safety risks to the
birds that have access to them.
The primary enclosure must be constructed and maintained so that they protect the birds from injury. Correct by
addressing the safety risks identified during the inspection.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

Various perches are in a state of disrepair and are inappropriate for the species. An outdoor enclosure containing two
adult Horned Screamers, an outdoor enclosure containing an adult Ocellated turkey, and an outdoor enclosure containing
two adult Ocellated turkeys provided perches consisting of 2”x4” wood boards mounted so that the 2-in side was facing
up. These perches are not appropriate in shape for these species.
Outdoor perimeter cage 2, containing two adult Helmeted Curassows, provided 2x2 square perches that were not
appropriate in shape for this species. Aviary 8, cage 3, containing one adult Black-Necked Aracari, provided a wood
dowel that had only one end securely mounted while the other had broken off and was freely moving. The rooftop
enclosure 8C, containing one adult Spectacled Owl, had a wooden horizontal board that was covered in algae and
showing signs of rot that could result in injury to the bird should the bird attempt to perch on the weakened wood and fall.
Aviary 17 cage 5 containing an Ornate Hawk, had a standalone feeding platform that was rotting, was coming apart at the
sides, and had exposed nails where the birds would be perching.
Improper perch size, shape, and texture can lead to health issues like pododermatitis and put strain on the bird’s feet and
legs.
If the enclosure houses birds that rest by perching, there must be perches available that are appropriate to the age and
species of the birds housed therein and a sufficient number of perches of appropriate size, shape, strength, texture and
placement to comfortably hold all the birds in the primary enclosure at the same time, including birds that are ranked low
in a dominance hierarchy.
Correct by September 1, 2026.

An outdoor enclosure containing an adult Blue-Billed Curassow identified as 25H048 had a recent gash on its beak.
Inspectors observed an adult Wattled Curassow in the enclosure adjacent to it actively attacking (striking and pecking
through the fence) the Blue-Billed.
Failure to adequately screen adjacent enclosures is causing injury to the Blue-Billed Curassow.
Primary enclosures that are adjacent to one another or that share a common side with another enclosure must be suitably
screened from each other or kept at a sufficient distance apart in order to prevent injury of the occupants due to predation,
territorial disputes, or aggression.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

citations.desc: Environment enhancement to promote psychological well-being.
citations.narrative:
The facility does not have an environmental enhancement plan (EEP) approved by the attending veterinarian. Many
enclosures were bare with only perches and their food receptacles present. Failure to implement and follow an EEP as
approved by the attending veterinarian as outlined can negatively impact the health and well-being of the animals.
Exhibitors must develop, document, and follow a species-appropriate plan for environmental enhancement that is
approved by the attending veterinarian to adequately promote the psychological well-being of birds.
Correct by August 7, 2026.

Food and food supplements provided by the facility were not wholesome and free of contamination. Multiple containers of
moldy papayas stored in the refrigerator intended for the use of the bird were moldy, softened, and discolored. The
Wisbroek Multipro Powder bird supplement kept among the other bird supplements expired in October 2023 and was still
in use. Feeding food and food supplements that is moldy, contaminated or expired may result in poor health.
The diet for birds must be wholesome, palatable, and free contamination.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
Inspectors observed unsanitary conditions in and around most bird enclosures and on water lines, characterized by heavy
accumulation of droppings, feather dust, and old food. Many perches, bars, and enclosure floors were covered in caked-
on debris. Such accumulation is detrimental to avian health. Excreta and food waste must be removed from the primary
enclosures and from under and around primary enclosures as often as necessary to prevent excessive accumulation of
feces and food waste, to prevent soiling of the birds contained in the primary enclosure, and to reduce disease hazards,
insects, pests, and odors.
Correct by August 5, 2026.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility is storing boxes of drinking cups for the aquarium in front of and on top of feed bags. Employees’ personal
items [medications, condiments, snacks, drinks] were scattered throughout the kitchen area and the indoor storage areas.
The upper-level storage areas had a disarray of transport cages among boxes of receipts, paperwork, and other random
equipment, and there were excessive spiderwebs in those areas. There were accumulations of wood panels, metal
panels, metal pipes and PVC pipes adjacent to several outdoor enclosures.
Failure to keep premises where housing facilities are located clean and in good repair may cause injury to the birds and
does not facilitate the required husbandry practices.
Premises where housing facilities are located, including buildings, surrounding grounds, and exhibit areas, must be kept
clean and in good repair in order to protect the birds from injury and disease, to facilitate the husbandry practices required
in this subpart, and to reduce or eliminate breeding and living areas for rodents, pests, and vermin.
Correct by August 18, 2026.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility’s current program for the control of insect and mammalian pests is ineffective.
Inspectors observed numerous cockroach bodies throughout the main building, in the delivery area for food and supplies
and under the cabinets and storage shelves in the kitchen, and throughout the walkways between the bird enclosures.
Cage 11 containing one geriatric Resplendent Quetzal in the main building [the last enclosure at the end of the walkway]
had a large accumulation of dead cockroaches on the floor of the enclosure. Inspectors observed live and dead
cockroaches throughout most outdoor bird enclosures, including behind the windowpane of the parrot enclosures. The
walk-in fridge containing flamingo feed had a vast amount of dead cockroaches. When inspectors opened the fridge door,
several bodies fell out.
Inspectors observed a dead mouse in several enclosures including, outdoor enclosure 17 with a Blue-Throated
Toucanette, aviary 8 containing various parrot species, and aviary 3 near cage 5 containing one Lesser bird of paradise. .
The outdoor enclosures for Horned Curassows behind the veterinary clinic had evidence of rodent activity throughout the
substrate in the form of various tunnels and openings in the substrate of their enclosure floors. The walk-in fridge
containing flamingo food had a deceased mouse present on the floor. Rodent feces were seen throughout the veterinary
clinic, the upper-level storage area for the flamingo feed, Aviary 20, and within the seals for the washer/dryer. Inspectors
observed rodent nests throughout the veterinary clinic and unused secondary kitchen ventilation ducts.
Ants were present throughout the kitchen where employees were actively prepping food for the birds. Extensive numbers
of ants were present in the fresh food, on food receptacles, and throughout enclosures for a vast majority of the outdoor
bird enclosures.
Although the facility sets traps and sprays, the current program is not effective as evidenced by the findings above. Pests
such as rodents, cockroaches and ants can adversely affect the health and well-being of the birds by spreading disease
and contaminating food, surfaces and animal housing areas. A safe and effective program for the control of insects,
ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests shall be established and maintained.
Correct by August 18, 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the facility representative.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
